# Bayesian estimation (MCMC)

`method = bayes` runs full MCMC Bayesian estimation — it draws from the joint
posterior

$$
p(\theta, \Omega, \Sigma, \{\eta_i\} \mid y) \propto
\Big[\prod_i p(y_i \mid \theta, \eta_i, \Sigma)\,\mathcal{N}(\eta_i \mid 0, \Omega)\Big]\;
p(\theta)\,p(\Omega)\,p(\Sigma)
$$

rather than returning a single point estimate. It targets parity with NONMEM
`METHOD=BAYES`. This is a **Gibbs-within-HMC** sampler (the "Path A" design): it
reuses the per-subject HMC/MH kernels and the conjugate sufficient statistics
the other estimators already build, so it needs no population-level gradient.

> **IOV.** Inter-occasion variability (per-occasion `kappa`) is supported for
> **zero-mean kappas** — `κ ~ N(0, Ω_iov)` added to an existing mu-reference, the
> `exp(η + κ)` form. Kappas that anchor to their own θ (kappa mu-references) are
> rejected.

## The sampler

Each sweep, for each chain, cycles these blocks:

1. **η block** — samples $\eta_i \mid \theta, \Omega, \Sigma, \kappa, y$ for
   every subject. The default is a Metropolis kernel that adapts **per subject**:
   block random-walk moves with the subject's own step size, shaped from
   mid-warmup by the subject's own running η covariance (rather than by the
   prior's $\mathrm{chol}(\Omega)$), followed by componentwise sweeps with a
   step per η. Gradient-guided **HMC** replaces it when requested
   (`n_leapfrog > 0`, an analytical-PK model, no IOV, no mixture). The HMC
   gradient is the exact analytic `Dual2` η-gradient — the same one FOCEI uses.
   Every chain starts each subject's η at its empirical Bayes estimate (EBE) at
   the initial parameters; see [Why the chains start at the EBEs](#why-the-chains-start-at-the-ebes).

1b. **κ block** (IOV models) — samples each per-occasion
   $\kappa_{ik} \mid \eta, \theta, \Omega, \Omega_{iov}, y$ holding η fixed.

2. **Ω block** — a conjugate **inverse-Wishart** draw
   $\Omega \mid \{\eta_i\} \sim \mathcal{W}^{-1}(\nu_0 + N,\ \Lambda_0 + \textstyle\sum_i \eta_i\eta_i^\top)$,
   with structural zeros / fixed entries re-imposed and the diagonal floored.

2c. **Ω_iov block** (IOV) — the same conjugate inverse-Wishart draw from the
   per-occasion kappa scatter $\textstyle\sum_i\sum_k \kappa_{ik}\kappa_{ik}^\top$.
   The posterior `OMEGA_IOV(i,j)` entries appear in the summaries.

3. **mu-referenced θ block** — for `P_i = θ·exp(η_i)` the population mean
   $\mu = \log\theta$ has the exact Gaussian full conditional
   $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{\text{old}} + \bar\eta,\ \Omega/N)$. The draw
   is applied as a shift $s$: $\theta \leftarrow \theta\,e^{s}$ and
   $\eta_i \leftarrow \eta_i - s$, which leaves each individual parameter
   $\log\varphi_i = \mu + \eta_i$ unchanged (only the η-prior moves). The
   draw is accepted by a Metropolis–Hastings step scored on the real
   likelihood. That step makes the move exact for any model, and when the
   assumptions above hold it accepts every draw, so the move is the Gibbs
   draw. This move is what gives the sampler good mixing. Covariate coefficients
   that enter $\log P_i$ linearly join it; see
   [Covariate coefficients](#covariate-coefficients). The move runs when every η
   is covered by a log mu-reference or such a covariate mu-reference.

4. **(remaining θ, σ) block** — a random-walk Metropolis step in unconstrained
   space (log where the lower bound is ≥ 0) for any θ the conjugate move does
   not draw and for σ, with objective $\sum_i \mathrm{nll}_i$ (η and Ω fixed,
   so the η-prior term cancels in the acceptance ratio).

Step sizes adapt during warmup toward a ~0.234 acceptance rate (0.44 for the
componentwise η moves). Post-warmup draws are thinned by `bayes_thin` and
summarized.

### Bounds

Every θ draw stays inside its declared `(lower, upper)` bounds. A random-walk
proposal or a conjugate draw that lands outside is rejected, and the chain
keeps its current value. The posterior density is zero outside the bounds, so
this is an exact Metropolis–Hastings step, and the prior stays the documented
one truncated to the bounds. Sampling on a transform of `(lower, upper)` would
also be exact, provided the change-of-variables Jacobian is included. It is
not used because rejection needs no transform at all, and it leaves the
proposal scales and the prior on the scale they are documented on. Until
issue #1626 the random-walk block ignored the bounds. A covariate exponent declared
`(0.75, 0.01, 5.0)` could then drift to 5e-9, where `(WT/70)^θ ≈ 1` leaves the
likelihood flat.

### Covariate coefficients

A covariate coefficient whose typical value is linear on the log scale has a
Gaussian full conditional, like the typical value itself:

```
CL = TVCL * (WT/70)^THETA_WT * (CRCL/100)^THETA_CRCL * exp(ETA_CL)
log CL_i = log TVCL + THETA_WT*log(WT_i/70) + THETA_CRCL*log(CRCL_i/100) + ETA_CL_i
```

That is a linear regression of the individual log-parameters on the
covariates. The conjugate move draws `log TVCL`, `THETA_WT` and `THETA_CRCL`
jointly from it, as it draws the typical values. A coefficient shared by
several parameters (`THETA_WT` on CL and V1) is one coordinate of that
regression. The move re-centres every η so the individual parameters are
unchanged. With a flat prior on the coordinates (log θ for a typical value, θ
for an exponent or slope), the precision is
$P = \sum_i X_i^\top \Omega^{-1} X_i$ and the mean is
$\beta + P^{-1}\sum_i X_i^\top\Omega^{-1}\eta_i$.

The Gaussian is exactly the full conditional only when the typical values
are linear in these coordinates and the data depend on the θ through the
individual parameters alone. The move does not rely on that. Each draw is a
proposal, accepted or rejected by a Metropolis–Hastings step that scores the
real likelihood with the same per-subject function every other block uses, so
the move targets the right posterior for any model. When the conditions hold,
the acceptance ratio is 1 to rounding (measured: |log α| ≤ 5e-12), and the
move is the exact Gibbs draw. When they do not, some draws are rejected; the
cost is mixing, not correctness. To keep acceptance high, a coefficient stays
on the random walk when any of these holds:

- a covariate it reads changes within a subject;
- the θ is read elsewhere in the model;
- the η is read by a second parameter;
- the typical value is not one of the recognised linear forms, e.g.
  `(TVCL + (CRCL - 90)*TH_CRCL) * exp(ETA_CL)`;
- the data cannot identify the coefficient through the individual parameters.
  This happens when every subject is at the covariate's reference value, or
  when the covariate is constant across subjects and so duplicates the
  typical value.

Linearity is judged from the written form of the typical value, not by
probing it numerically. An odd term such as `(θ - θ₀)^3` passes every
symmetric check about θ₀. The recognised forms are products and quotients of
θ and constants, powers with a constant base or a constant exponent, and
`exp()` of a linear term. Under the logit and identity links they are sums of
constant multiples of θ. `log`, `ln` and `sqrt` of a θ-dependent argument are
not recognised. The DSL evaluates them clamped (`ln(max(x, 1e-30))` and
`sqrt(max(x, 0))`), so `log(exp(θ·c))` is flat below the floor rather than
linear.

**Prior.** Moving a coefficient onto this move changes its prior. On the
random walk it has the default N(init, sd = 10) on log θ, truncated to its
bounds. On the conjugate move it has a flat prior on θ itself, truncated to
its bounds. The posteriors are comparable whenever the data dominate. A
coefficient the data barely inform will show the difference.

**Acceptance is reported.** Because rejection is harmless to correctness, a
move that is rejected every sweep looks exactly like one that is working. It
is not: a θ this move draws is taken out of the random-walk (θ, σ) block, so
nothing else proposes it, and a chain that never accepts leaves that θ at its
initial value for the whole run. The fit therefore warns when the move
accepted fewer than half of its post-warmup draws, and names the largest group
of rejections — a draw outside a declared bound, a Metropolis rejection, or a
conditional that could not be formed at all.

The rate is judged **per chain**, and the chain with the worst rate decides.
Pooling would hide the case worth reporting: one dead chain among four pools
to 75% and says nothing, while a quarter of the posterior sample holds a
frozen coordinate. On a recognised linear form with no active bound every
chain accepts every draw.

Mixture models draw only the plain typical values.

### Why the chains start at the EBEs

On `two_cpt_oral_base`, one subject's posterior has a second mode: the KA ↔
distribution flip-flop, $e^{-19.6}$ times less probable than the main mode.
The ratio comes from a Laplace approximation at the posterior means. Started
from η = 0, a chain could fall into the second mode in warmup. No random-walk
kernel climbs back out, so the run reported max R̂ ≈ 1.2 at 1,000, 6,000 and
20,000 draws per chain alike. On this example, starting at the EBE (here the
main mode) removed the trap: R̂ ≤ 1.008 across four seeds. Like the shared
initial θ, the start does not change the target distribution, only where the
chains begin. Mixture models keep η = 0, because their EBE is per class.

The start has a diagnostic cost:

- **An EBE is a local optimum.** It is not guaranteed to be the dominant
  mode.
- **The chains all start in the same place.** Every chain begins at the same
  EBEs and the same initial θ. If they all stay in one mode, R̂ and ESS can
  look reassuring while every chain misses another mode.

A max R̂ near 1 from common starts therefore shows the chains agree. It does
not show they have explored the whole posterior. For a model where a second
mode is plausible, refit from different initial estimates and compare the
posteriors.

## Options

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|-----|--------:|---------|
| `bayes_warmup` | 1000 | Warmup (burn-in + adaptation) sweeps per chain, discarded. |
| `bayes_iters`  | 1000 | Retained sampling sweeps per chain (before thinning). |
| `bayes_chains` | 4 | Independent chains (distinct seeds; used for split-R̂). |
| `bayes_thin`   | 1 | Keep every `bayes_thin`-th sampling draw. |
| `bayes_seed`   | — | Base RNG seed; chain `c` derives its own. |
| `n_leapfrog`   | 0 | Leapfrog steps for the HMC η kernel (analytical-PK models; `0` ⇒ the adaptive Metropolis kernel). |
| `n_mh_steps`   | auto | Block Metropolis moves per subject per sweep; the componentwise sweeps are sized from it. |

## Output

Posterior summaries are reported on `FitResult.bayes` and in the `.fit.yaml`
`bayes:` section — per parameter: `mean`, `sd`, `q025`, `median`, `q975`,
split-`rhat`, `ess_bulk` / `ess_tail`, and `mcse`; plus `n_chains`, `n_warmup`,
`n_draws_per_chain`, `n_divergent`, and `max_rhat`. The point-estimate fields
(`theta`/`omega`/`sigma`) carry the posterior means; the covariance / SIR steps
are skipped (posterior credible intervals replace the Hessian covariance).

A `max_rhat` above ~1.01 indicates the chains have not converged. This is also
the threshold for the reported `converged` flag. The warning names the
parameter with the worst R̂ and gives advice for the block that samples it:

- **A random-walk θ** (a θ the conjugate move does not draw). Longer chains
  rarely help, because the data pin such a θ at fixed η. The warning suggests
  mu-referencing it, or writing its covariate effect linearly on the log scale.
  If it already is log mu-referenced, the conjugate move is off because some
  other η is not covered.
- **An Ω entry or a conjugate-drawn θ, under the Metropolis η kernel, on a
  model HMC can serve.** The warning suggests `n_leapfrog`.
- **Anything else.** The warning suggests increasing `bayes_warmup` /
  `bayes_iters`. Use **at least 2 chains** (`bayes_chains >= 2`): split-R̂ on a
single chain only compares the two halves of one trajectory and cannot detect
between-chain non-convergence, so a near-1 `max_rhat` from one chain is weak
evidence; a single-chain run is warned about for this reason.

## Example

```toml
[fit_options]
  method       = bayes
  bayes_warmup = 1000
  bayes_iters  = 2000
  bayes_chains = 4
  bayes_seed   = 1
```

```
--- Bayesian posterior (Gibbs-within-HMC) ---
  chains = 4, warmup = 1000, draws/chain = 2000, max R-hat = 1.002
  param              mean         sd       2.5%      97.5%   Rhat      ESS
  TVCL             0.1329     0.0081     0.1172     0.1496  1.000     7900
  TVV              7.7445     0.2858     7.2093     8.3310  1.000     7960
  TVKA             0.8280     0.1620     0.5605     1.1975  1.000     7930
```

## Priors

Defaults are weakly-informative (≈ flat given typical data): $\Omega \sim
\mathcal{W}^{-1}(n_\eta + 2,\ \Omega_0)$ centred at the initial Ω, and
$\theta,\ \log\sigma \sim \mathcal{N}(\text{init},\ \mathrm{sd}=10)$ on the
unconstrained scale. The θ the conjugate mu-reference move draws have a flat
prior on their linear scale (log θ for a typical value, θ for a covariate
coefficient). All θ priors are truncated to the declared bounds.
User-specifiable priors in the `.ferx` DSL are planned.

## Validation

### Two-compartment examples (#1626)

On the ferx-r examples `two_cpt_oral_base` and `two_cpt_oral_cov` (30 subjects,
`data/two_cpt_oral_cov.csv`), with 4 chains on Linux:

| model, draws per chain | before: max R̂ / min bulk ESS | after: max R̂ / min bulk ESS |
|---|---|---|
| base, 1,000 (defaults) | 1.194 / 7 | 1.006 / 609 |
| base, 6,000 | 1.197 / 7 | 1.001 / 2,694 |
| cov, 1,000 (defaults) | 2.735 / 3 | 1.017 / 482 |
| cov, 6,000 | 7.158 / 2 | 1.002 / 2,951 |

At the defaults, the base model gives max R̂ 1.005–1.008 across the default
seed and seeds 1–3 (before: 1.19–2.04), and none of them warns. The covariate
model varies more between seeds in these short runs:

| seed | max R̂ / min bulk ESS |
|---|---|
| default | 1.017 / 482 |
| 1 | 1.004 |
| 2 | 1.005 |
| 3 | 1.014 / 505 |

Two of the four seeds warn. If you are warned, run longer chains. At 6,000
draws per chain the default seed gives 1.002 with ESS 2,951 and no warning.
The worst parameter is usually σ (`PROP_ERR`), which the random-walk block
samples. The
posterior means sit within 0.12 posterior SD of the FOCEI estimates for every
θ and σ, for example:

| parameter | FOCEI | Bayes mean (6,000 per chain) |
|---|---:|---:|
| base TVV1 | 48.32 | 48.07 |
| base TVKA | 1.257 | 1.253 |
| cov THETA_WT | 0.654 | 0.665 |
| cov THETA_CRCL | 0.565 | 0.571 |

The Ω means sit above the MLE, as on warfarin. Warfarin itself is unchanged:
max R̂ 1.002–1.004 and min bulk ESS 847–986 across four seeds (before:
1.001–1.008, 619–862).

### Warfarin

On the bundled warfarin model the posterior means match the FOCEI point estimate
and NONMEM `METHOD=BAYES` (TVCL ≈ 0.133, TVV ≈ 7.74, TVKA ≈ 0.83), with
`max_rhat` ≈ 1.00. Ω posterior means run slightly above the MLE — the expected
inverse-Wishart posterior-mean bias at small subject counts.

> NONMEM reports `SIGMA` as the variance of `EPS`; ferx parameterises
> proportional error as $\mathrm{Var} = (f\sigma)^2$ and reports σ as the
> SD, so compare `ferx σ ≈ √(NONMEM SIGMA)`.
